To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
guarantees may be good, bad or neutral for financial stability.

(i) guarantees reduce bank risk taking, (ii) this reduction in risk taking might increase the probability of a bank run, (iii) guarantees against fundamental based runs and panic based runs are more efficient than guarantees against panic alone and (iv) guarantees might reduce bank risk taking below the optimal level
government guarantees to financial institutions can increase the probability of a bank run and that the optimal policy is not to guarantee panic based runs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the government can best use its limited resources to provide guarantees that reduce the probability of runs without increasing bank risk taking.
the role of guarantees as a tool to improve bank stability and the efficiency of the financial system.
the role of government guarantees in financial markets, and the trade offs involved.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of guarantees on bank risk taking and the probability of a bank failure depend on many factors, and that the net effect is not necessarily a negative one.
guarantees may be welfare increasing, but only if the government can credibly commit to not bailing out banks that take excessive risk.
guarantees are good, but not always.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
guarantees are a second best instrument, but that the best second best instrument may not be the one that reduces the likelihood of bank runs.
the introduction of guarantees is likely to be beneficial if the probability of a bank failure is high, but not necessarily so if the probability is low.
government guarantees are a second best solution to financial crises and bank failures.
The main takeaway from our work is that

government guarantees are a double edge sword: while reducing the probability of bank failures and runs they also lead to excessive bank risk taking and distortions in banks incentives to monitor borrowers.
guarantees may have ambiguous effects on the likelihood of a run and the amount of bank lending.
the effects of guarantees on the likelihood of bank runs and on the level of risk taking depend on the type of guarantee and on the type of failure.
